node.label: Paul Thompson
node.description: A social and oral historian concerned with how interviews change both historical evidence and research practice. His retrospective interview credits Townsend’s socially engaged research and George Ewart Evans’s listening methods, and recalls resisting Hobsbawm’s request to remove oral-history material from The Edwardians. Thompson distinguishes his early emphasis on reliable recollection from later attention to subjectivity, silence and memory associated with Passerini and Portelli. His community-history discussion also warns that participation can exclude less confident people and need not produce progressive politics. Becky Taylor’s reassessment credits the fishing project’s attention to change and its preservation of sources, while questioning interview schedules, uneven transcription and the insufficiently examined category of fisherman. Her reuse demonstrates how an archive can support questions its makers did not fully pursue. Living the Fishing was collaborative work with Tony Wailey and Trevor Lummis, not Thompson’s solitary project.
